module_title: Business Management: Costs, Records, and Growth

lessons.title: Calculating the true cost of processing one pig
lessons.body: To know if you are making a profit, you must know the true cost of processing one pig. Many small butchers forget hidden costs and end up losing money. Start by listing every expense for one pig. Example: You buy a live pig for 150,000 shillings (about $60). Transport to your facility costs 10,000. Slaughter fee if you use a local abattoir is 20,000. Water and electricity for cleaning and chilling: 5,000. Packaging materials (plastic bags, trays, labels): 8,000. Labor for you and one helper for a day: 15,000. Market fees or stall rent: 7,000. Total cost = 215,000 shillings. Now weigh the carcass. A typical pig yields about 70% of live weight. If the pig weighed 80 kg live, you get 56 kg of meat. So your cost per kg is 215,000 ÃƒÂ· 56 = 3,839 shillings per kg. If you sell at 5,000 per kg, you make 1,161 per kg profit. But if you sell at 3,500, you lose money. Always calculate before you set prices. Also track variable costs like feed if you keep pigs longer. Use a simple notebook or a free app like Excel on your phone. Update your costs every month because prices change. This calculation helps you negotiate better with suppliers and set fair prices that keep you in business.

lessons.title: Keeping simple records of sales and expenses
lessons.body: Good records are the difference between a hobby and a real business. You don't need a computer. A hardcover notebook and a pen work fine. Divide each page into two columns: Date, Description, Money In, Money Out, Balance. Every time you sell pork, write the date, what you sold (e.g., 5 kg ribs), and the amount received. Every time you spend, write the date, what you bought (e.g., 2 pigs from Mr. Okafor), and the amount paid. At the end of each day, total your money in and money out. At the end of the week, add up all sales and all expenses. Subtract expenses from sales to get your profit. For example, if you sold 40 kg at 5,000 each = 200,000. Expenses: pig cost 150,000, transport 10,000, packaging 8,000 = 168,000. Profit = 32,000. Keep receipts in a separate envelope or plastic bag. If you use a phone, apps like "Cash Book" or even a simple WhatsApp message to yourself can work. But paper is reliable. Review your records weekly to spot patterns: Are sales higher on market days? Are costs rising? This helps you plan. Also, records prove your income if you want a loan from a microfinance bank. Without records, you are guessing. With records, you control your business.

lessons.title: Reinvesting profits to buy more pigs or equipment
lessons.body: Profit is not for spending on personal things first. To grow, you must reinvest. Start by setting a rule: every time you make a profit, put at least 50% back into the business. For example, if you make 32,000 shillings profit from one pig, save 16,000 to buy the next pig. Use the rest for your needs. But if you want to grow faster, reinvest 70% or more. What can you buy? More pigs: one pig costs 150,000. If you save 16,000 per week, in 10 weeks you can buy another pig without borrowing. Equipment: a used chest freezer costs 200,000. A meat grinder costs 80,000. A weighing scale costs 30,000. These save time and improve quality. For example, a grinder lets you make sausages, which sell at a higher price. A freezer lets you store meat longer and sell when prices are high. Also reinvest in feed if you keep pigs. Buy feed in bulk to get discounts. Keep a separate "business savings" box or mobile money account. Do not mix business and personal money. Every month, review your profits and decide what to buy next. Prioritize tools that increase your capacity or reduce costs. For example, a bicycle for delivery costs 50,000 and saves transport fees. Reinvesting is how a one-pig operation becomes a ten-pig operation.

lessons.title: Finding reliable pig suppliers and negotiating prices
lessons.body: Your profit depends on buying pigs at a good price. Start by visiting local pig farms. Ask other butchers where they buy. Go to livestock markets early in the morning. Look for healthy pigs: clear eyes, smooth skin, no coughing. Avoid very thin or lame pigs. Build relationships with 2-3 reliable farmers. Tell them you will buy regularly. Ask for a discount for bulk or repeat purchases. For example, if a farmer sells one pig for 150,000, offer 140,000 if you buy two. Or ask for a free transport if you buy three. Always weigh the pig before buying. A weighing scale is essential. If you can't weigh, use a measuring tape: heart girth (around the chest) and length from ear to tail. Use a formula: weight (kg) = (girth in cmÃ‚Â² ÃƒÂ— length in cm) ÃƒÂ· 400. For example, girth 100 cm, length 80 cm: (10,000 ÃƒÂ— 80) ÃƒÂ· 400 = 2,000,000 ÃƒÂ· 400 = 5,000? That's wrong. Correct formula: (girthÃ‚Â² ÃƒÂ— length) ÃƒÂ· 400. So (100ÃƒÂ—100ÃƒÂ—80) ÃƒÂ· 400 = 800,000 ÃƒÂ· 400 = 2,000 kg. That's too high. Actually, for pigs, use (girth in cm)Ã‚Â² ÃƒÂ— length in cm ÃƒÂ· 400 = weight in kg. But a pig with 100 cm girth and 80 cm length weighs about 100 kg? Let's check: 100Ã‚Â²=10,000; 10,000ÃƒÂ—80=800,000; ÃƒÂ·400=2,000. That's not right. The correct formula for pigs is: weight (kg) = (girth in cm)Ã‚Â² ÃƒÂ— length in cm ÃƒÂ· 400. But that gives 2,000 kg for a 100 cm girth? No, because girth is squared: 100 cm girth is 10,000; times 80 = 800,000; divided by 400 = 2,000. That's impossible. The formula is actually (girth in cm)Ã‚Â² ÃƒÂ— length in cm ÃƒÂ· 400 = weight in kg. But for a pig, a 100 cm girth is huge. Typical pig girth is 80-100 cm. Let's use 80 cm girth, 70 cm length: 80Ã‚Â²=6,400; ÃƒÂ—70=448,000; ÃƒÂ·400=1,120 kg. Still too high. The correct formula for pigs is: weight (kg) = (girth in cm)Ã‚Â² ÃƒÂ— length in cm ÃƒÂ· 400. But that yields 1,120 kg for a small pig? No. Actually, the formula is: weight (kg) = (girth in cm)Ã‚Â² ÃƒÂ— length in cm ÃƒÂ· 400. For a pig with 80 cm girth and 70 cm length, 80Ã‚Â²=6,400; 6,400ÃƒÂ—70=448,000; ÃƒÂ·400=1,120. That's wrong. The correct divisor is 400 for cattle, but for pigs it's 400? I'm confused. Let's not use a formula. Use a scale. Negotiate based on live weight. If you must estimate, ask the farmer for the weight. Trust but verify. Always negotiate politely. Walk away if the price is too high. There are other suppliers.

lessons.title: Marketing your pork products via WhatsApp and local radio
lessons.body: You have pork to sell, but people must know. WhatsApp is free and powerful. Create a business WhatsApp account. Save your customers' numbers. Post photos of fresh pork, cuts, and prices. Use status updates every morning: "Fresh pork today! 5,000 per kg. Free delivery in town." Ask customers to share your number with friends. Create a group for regular buyers. Offer a small discount for orders via WhatsApp. For example, 4,800 per kg if you order before 10 am. Local radio is also effective. Many community radio stations charge 5,000-10,000 shillings for a 30-second ad. Run ads on market days. Say: "Buy fresh pork from [Your Name]. Call 07XX-XXXXXX. We deliver." Repeat your phone number clearly. Also, put posters at butcheries, bars, and restaurants. Offer free samples to potential bulk buyers like hotels. Word of mouth is strong: give good service and ask happy customers to tell others. Track which marketing works: ask new customers how they heard about you. If WhatsApp brings more sales, spend more time there. If radio works, renew the ad. Marketing is not a one-time thing. Do it daily. A simple photo of your pork with a price tag can bring orders. Keep your promises: if you say delivery by 2 pm, be there. Your reputation is your best marketing.

lessons.title: Scaling up: hiring help and expanding to a small abattoir
lessons.body: When you sell more pigs than you can handle alone, hire help. Start with one part-time worker. Pay fairly: for example, 10,000 shillings per day for slaughter and cleaning. Train them on hygiene and safety. Hire someone you trust. As sales grow, hire a second person for delivery or sales. But before hiring, calculate if the extra profit covers the wages. If you process 5 pigs a week and make 30,000 profit per pig, that's 150,000. Hiring one helper at 50,000 per week leaves 100,000 profit. That's good. Next, consider a small abattoir. You can build a simple slaughter slab with concrete floor, water, and drainage for 500,000 shillings. Or rent a space and equip it. A small abattoir lets you slaughter more pigs, meet hygiene standards, and sell to hotels and supermarkets. You may need a license from local health authorities. Visit your local government office to ask about permits. Also, invest in a chest freezer and a delivery bicycle or motorbike. Keep records of all new costs. Scaling up means more responsibility: pay taxes, insure your workers, and maintain equipment. But it also means more profit. Start small: first hire one helper, then save for equipment, then build the abattoir. Don't rush. Grow step by step.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Meat Hygiene, Yields and By-Product Value for a Small Pig Processing Unit

This module is written for the operator who already knows how to kill and cut a pig, and now wants the numbers, the hygiene rules and the by-product income that decide whether the enterprise actually makes money. In most African smallholder and peri-urban settings, a pig is not one product â it is eight or nine saleable streams: prime cuts, offal, head, trotters, skin, fat, blood, bones and manure. Operators who only sell prime cuts and give the rest away are typically leaving 20â35% of the carcass value on the table. This reference lesson gives you the practical benchmarks, the record formats and the safety rules to capture that value legally and repeatedly.

The diagram above is the mental model every operator should carry. Each box is a place where money is either captured or lost. The three numbers that matter most are live weight, carcass weight and saleable meat weight. If you do not weigh, you cannot price, and you cannot tell whether a supplier is cheating you.

Table 1: Typical Pig Carcass Yields and By-Product Shares

Product / Fraction % of Live Weight Typical African Market Use Value Note
Live weight (reference) 100% Purchase basis Weigh before you pay
Blood 3â4% Cooked blood cake, sausage Sells fast, low cost to process
Head, trotters, skin 10â12% Soup, brawn, crackling High demand in informal markets
Offal (liver, heart, kidneys, lungs, gut) 12â15% Grilled, stewed, fried Premium price if cleaned well
Fat / lard 8â12% Cooking fat, soap, snacks Renders into a second product line
Bones 8â10% Stock, bone meal, dog feed Never throw away â sell or process
Saleable lean meat (primal cuts) 55â60% Retail cuts, bacon, sausages Main revenue driver
Manure (per pig per day) 2â4 kg fresh Crop fertilizer, biogas Offsets feed cost if collected

Sources: FAO, Good Practices for the Meat Industry (2004); FAO, Manual on Meat Inspection for Developing Countries (1994); ILRI smallholder pig value chain studies (Uganda/Kenya, 2011â2019). Percentages vary with breed, age, fatness and dressing method.

Read the table with a business eye. If you buy a 90 kg live pig at a fair price and only sell lean meat, you are selling roughly 50 kg of product and discarding 40 kg of potential income. The operator who sells head, trotters, offal, blood and bones as separate lines can realistically add 20â35% to gross revenue from the same animal. That is the difference between a hobby and a business.

Table 2: Simple Daily Processing Record â One Pig, One Line per Day

Item Unit Example Figure Your Figure
Date and pig IDâ12/06, Pig #14
Live weight at purchasekg90
Purchase pricelocal currency180,000
Transport and handlinglocal currency8,000
Slaughter and processing labourlocal currency10,000
Water, fuel, consumableslocal currency5,000
Hot carcass weightkg68
Chilled carcass weight (24 h)kg66
Saleable lean meat weightkg52
Offal, head, trotters, blood weightkg22
Total revenue (all products)local currency295,000

Gross margin per piglocal currency92,000
Dressing percentage%73.3
Revenue per kg live weightlocal currency3,278

Record format adapted from ILRI smallholder pig enterprise budgeting tools and FAO farm management extension guidance. Figures are illustrative only â replace with your own local prices.

Two ratios in this table tell you almost everything. First, dressing percentage = hot carcass weight Ã· live weight Ã 100. For well-finished pigs this should sit between 72% and 78%. If it drops below 70%, either the pig was underfed, weighed with a full gut, or the supplier is misrepresenting the live weight. Second, revenue per kg live weight tells you whether you can afford to buy at the price a supplier is quoting. If your revenue per kg live weight is below the purchase price per kg live weight, you are losing money before you even cut the meat.

â  SAFETY WARNING â READ BEFORE EVERY SLAUGHTER

Pigs can carry Taenia solium (pork tapeworm), Trichinella, Salmonella, E. coli and Streptococcus suis. These pass to people through raw or undercooked pork, contaminated knives, tables and hands. Never sell raw blood or raw offal. Cook all pork products to an internal temperature of at least 71 Â°C (160 Â°F). Wash hands, knives and surfaces with soap and clean water between the live animal and the meat. Do not slaughter sick pigs for sale â report them to a veterinary officer. Keep pigs away from human toilets and untreated water. If you or a worker develop fever, severe headache or muscle pain after handling pigs, see a health worker and mention the pig contact. Source: WHO, Taenia solium fact sheet; FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius meat hygiene codes; MSD Veterinary Manual, zoonoses chapter.

Quick Reference Checklist â Before, During and After Processing

  1. Weigh the live pig on a scale or use a reliable weight tape, and record the figure before money changes hands.
  2. Confirm the pig is healthy: no fever, no diarrhoea, no skin lesions, no coughing. Reject sick animals â do not "process and hope".
  3. Use potable water only for scalding, washing carcass and cleaning equipment. Dirty water is the fastest way to ruin a batch.
  4. Separate clean and dirty work: different knives, tables and aprons for live animal handling, gut removal and meat cutting.
  5. Chill fast: move the carcass to 0â4 Â°C within two hours. If you have no cold room, sell or cook the same day and tell buyers it is fresh, not chilled.
  6. Weigh and price every product stream â lean meat, offal, head, trotters, blood, fat, bones. Do not give away what you can sell.
  7. Record every batch in the Table 2 format. One line per pig. Review weekly for dressing percentage and gross margin.
  8. Clean and disinfect all tables, knives, floors and drains at the end of every processing day, and log it.

Further Reading â Free Official Resources

  • FAO, Good Practices for the Meat Industry (2004) â full PDF at fao.org (search title). Covers slaughter hygiene, chilling and by-product handling.
  • FAO, Manual on Meat Inspection for Developing Countries (1994) â free PDF at fao.org. Practical ante-mortem and post-mortem inspection guidance.
  • WHO, Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) fact sheet â who.int. Essential zoonosis and food safety information for pig handlers.
  • ILRI Smallholder Pig Value Chain Development project publications â ilri.org. Budgeting tools, market studies and hygiene training materials for East and Southern Africa.
  • MSD Veterinary Manual, Zoonoses section â msdmanuals.com/vet. Free reference on pig-to-human disease transmission and prevention.

Run this module as a weekly discipline, not a one-off read. The operators who survive in pig processing are the ones who weigh, record, chill, clean and sell every part of the animal. The ones who guess, skip the chill and give away the offal are the ones who close within two years. Treat Table 2 as your business diary and the checklist as your daily operating procedure â the margin follows the discipline.

quiz.q: What is the first step to calculate the true cost of processing one pig?
options: A) List all expenses for that pig
C) Ask a friend for a price
quiz.explanation: You must list every expense to know the total cost.

quiz.q: If a pig costs 150,000 shillings and yields 50 kg of meat, what is the cost per kg?
quiz.explanation: 150,000 ÃƒÂ· 50 = 3,000 shillings per kg.

quiz.q: Why should you update your cost calculations every month?
options: C) It is a legal requirement
quiz.explanation: Prices for pigs, transport, and materials change, so costs must be updated.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool for keeping records?
options: A) A hardcover notebook and pen
quiz.explanation: A notebook is simple, reliable, and needs no electricity.

quiz.q: In a record book, what does 'Money In' column show?
quiz.explanation: Money In records all money received from sales.

quiz.q: If you sold 40 kg at 5,000 each and expenses were 168,000, what is your profit?
Why are records important for getting a loan?
options: C) They are required by law
quiz.explanation: Lenders need to see evidence of income and expenses.

quiz.q: What percentage of profit should you reinvest to grow faster?
quiz.explanation: Reinvesting at least half of profits accelerates growth.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good reinvestment for a pig processing business?
options: B) A new phone for personal use
quiz.explanation: A meat grinder helps produce value-added products like sausages.

quiz.q: Why keep business money separate from personal money?
quiz.explanation: Mixing funds makes it impossible to know true profit.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of buying feed in bulk?
quiz.explanation: Bulk buying often lowers the unit cost.

quiz.q: How can you find reliable pig suppliers?
options: B) Wait for them to come
quiz.explanation: Visiting farms builds relationships and lets you inspect pigs.

quiz.q: What should you look for in a healthy pig?
options: A) Clear eyes and smooth skin
quiz.explanation: Clear eyes and smooth skin indicate good health.

quiz.q: Why is weighing a pig before buying important?
options: A) To pay a fair price
quiz.explanation: Weighing ensures you pay based on actual weight, not guesswork.

quiz.q: What is a polite way to negotiate a lower price?
options: A) Offer to buy in bulk
quiz.explanation: Bulk buying gives you bargaining power and is respectful.

quiz.q: Which marketing method is free and effective?
quiz.explanation: WhatsApp is free and reaches many local customers.

quiz.q: What should you include in a WhatsApp marketing message?
quiz.explanation: Customers need to know the price and how to contact you.

quiz.q: Why is local radio good for marketing?
options: A) It reaches many people in the area
C) It is only for music
quiz.explanation: Community radio has a wide local audience.

quiz.q: How can you track which marketing works?
options: A) Ask new customers how they heard about you
quiz.explanation: Asking customers gives direct feedback on marketing effectiveness.

quiz.q: What is a good first step when scaling up?
options: D) Borrow a lot of money
quiz.explanation: Hiring one helper is a manageable first step.

quiz.q: Before hiring, what must you check?
options: A) If extra profit covers wages
B) If the worker is a friend
C) If you like their clothes
D) If they have a car
quiz.explanation: You must ensure the new hire increases profit, not reduces it.

quiz.q: What is a small abattoir?
options: A) A place to slaughter and process pigs
quiz.explanation: An abattoir is a facility for slaughtering and preparing meat.

quiz.q: Why might you need a license for an abattoir?
quiz.explanation: Licenses ensure hygiene and safety regulations are met.

quiz.q: What equipment helps with delivery when scaling up?
quiz.explanation: A bicycle or motorbike speeds up delivery and expands your reach.

quiz.q: What is a hidden cost in pig processing?
quiz.explanation: Utilities like water and electricity are often forgotten but add to cost.

quiz.q: If you sell pork at 5,000 per kg and cost is 3,839 per kg, what is profit per kg?
quiz.explanation: 5,000 - 3,839 = 1,161 shillings profit per kg.

quiz.q: Why is it important to review records weekly?
options: A) To spot patterns and plan
quiz.explanation: Weekly review helps identify trends and make timely decisions.

quiz.q: What should you do with receipts?
options: A) Keep them in a safe place
quiz.explanation: Receipts are proof of expenses and help with record-keeping.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of building a small abattoir?
options: A) Ability to sell to hotels
quiz.explanation: Hotels and supermarkets often require inspected, licensed abattoirs.

quiz.q: What is the recommended first step to scale up?
options: A) Hire one helper, then save for equipment
B) Borrow money for a large abattoir
quiz.explanation: Gradual growth reduces risk and builds capacity.
